title_content.content: Asian Banks
After two decades of cost discipline, what's next for Asian banks?
AI as the next phase of cost efficiency

paragraph_content.content: Asian banks have spent the past two decades relying heavily on cost discipline to offset structural revenue headwinds, with meaningful but incomplete success in our view. As traditional efficiency levers mature, we believe AI now represents the most important opportunity to drive structural cost efficiencies, albeit with likely limited near-term P&L impact as deployments remain incremental. Our key takeaways are threefold: 1) historical cost efficiency gains have cushioned, but not fully offset, revenue pressure; 2) AI's medium-term impact will likely be highly uneven across markets and banks, driven by structural readiness rather than technology availability alone; and 3) despite this, AI optionality appears largely unpriced, with little differentiation at the sector, market or bank level today. Over time, we see scope for AI readiness to emerge as a driver of valuation divergence (please refer to our companion APAC Focus note here).

title_content.content: Cost efficiency has been the primary offset – but insufficient

paragraph_content.content: Over the past 20 years, banks have used cost efficiency as the dominant lever to defend profitability, with opex-to-assets declining materially across most Asian markets. These gains have been driven by banking consolidation, branch rationalisation, process automation and tighter headcount discipline. Banks have also invested heavily in technology over this period; however, much of this spend has largely focused on maintaining competitiveness and operational stability, with limited evidence of step-change cost savings at the system level. As a result, cost savings have only partially offset structural revenue pressure at an aggregate level.

title_content.content: AI adoption is accelerating, but near-term P&L impact remains limited

paragraph_content.content: AI adoption across Asian banks is accelerating, but current deployments remain narrow and largely siloed, focused on use cases such as customer servicing, compliance monitoring, credit assessments and internal productivity tools. As with past waves of technology investment, near-term financial benefits tend to show up as capacity release, risk reduction or cost avoidance rather than explicit cost cuts. In many cases, productivity gains are reinvested into further digitalisation, data infrastructure or compliance requirements. As a result, evidence of a consistent and material near-term P&L uplift from AI remains mixed, reinforcing our view that the early phase of AI adoption is evolutionary rather than transformative.

title_content.content: Medium term: AI as the scalable efficiency lever

paragraph_content.content: Looking ahead, we see AI as the most meaningful lever to drive structural cost efficiencies over the medium term, particularly given that operations and labour account for roughly 60–70% of banks' total cost bases. We believe successful, end-to-end AI integration has the potential to decouple revenue growth from headcount and physical infrastructure, allowing digitally enabled labour to scale at very low marginal cost. However, the ability to realise these gains will vary materially across markets and institutions, depending on factors such as scale, technology culture, data infrastructure, labour flexibility and competitive urgency. While execution risks are significant, higher AI readiness may help sustain relative cost and valuation advantages even as cyclical tailwinds fade.

title_content.content: Executive summary

paragraph_content.content: Asian banks are facing structural revenue headwinds driven by demographics-led pressure on net interest income (NII) and persistent challenges in scaling fee income. While operating cost discipline over the past two decades has been meaningful, we think it has not been sufficient to fully offset revenue erosion, raising the key question of whether AI can unlock the next leg of sustainable efficiency gains.

title_content.content: 1. Structural revenue pressure is real – and persistent

paragraph_content.content: Asian banks are facing increasingly structural revenue headwinds (revenue/assets fell 60bps over the past 20 years), driven primarily by demographic pressures that are weighing on traditional banking income streams.
Ageing populations across the region are slowing deposit accumulation and loan growth, compressing net interest margins and placing net interest income on a long-term downtrend.

Over the past two decades, net interest income as a percentage of assets has declined materially across Asia, while efforts to pivot toward non-interest income have delivered limited relief. Regulatory constraints, structural market features and competitive intensity have made fee income difficult to scale, resulting in a decline in fee income/ assets at the regional level.
Taken together, total revenue/assets has fallen meaningfully over the past 20 years, reinforcing our view that revenue pressures facing Asian banks are structural rather than cyclical in nature.

title_content.content: 2. Cost efficiency has helped – but only partially

paragraph_content.content: Against this backdrop, banks have leaned heavily on cost discipline to protect profitability. Operating efficiency has improved steadily over the past two decades, with total operating expenses/assets declining (~40bps over the past 20y) across most Asian markets.
However, these cost savings have only partially offset the revenue decline. At the aggregate level, lower operating expenses have compensated for roughly
of the fall in revenues, and have not fully insulated bottom-line profitability.

There is also a clear divergence across regions: emerging market banks have, on average, more than offset revenue pressure through cost reductions, while developed market banks have only been able to offset around
of the revenue decline.

Cost-to-income ratios have converged across Asia, with both developed and emerging market banks now operating at broadly similar levels, contrary to the common perception that emerging market banks are structurally less efficient.

title_content.content: 3. What drove past cost improvements?

paragraph_content.content: The sources of past efficiency gains suggest many traditional cost levers are now approaching maturity.

Staff costs account for just under half of total operating expenses, and while they have been a key driver of cost reduction in emerging markets, their contribution has been more limited in developed markets.

Other operating expenses, including branch, administrative and IT costs, have been the primary source of efficiency gains for developed market banks, reflecting consolidation and branch rationalisation.

While branch networks have been significantly reduced across most Asian markets in recent years, total bank headcount has, interestingly, continued to rise in many countries, likely driven by a shift away from customer-facing roles toward technology, data and back-office functions.

At the same time, technology spending has continued to increase, with Asian banks now spending around 4–5% of revenues on technology on average, and materially more in markets such as Singapore, Australia and Taiwan.

Furthermore, past tech investments have generally not resulted in a big improvement in operational efficiency for the sector. Many banks that increased their tech spend over the past 5 years are yet to see any reduction in their total opex to assets.

title_content.content: 4. AI adoption: strong momentum, limited near-term P&L impact

paragraph_content.content: AI adoption is accelerating rapidly across Asian banks, but its near-term financial impact remains limited in our view. Banks are increasingly deploying generative and agentic AI across customer engagement, internal productivity and risk management.

However, from a P&L perspective, these initiatives have so far delivered more in the form of capacity release and cost avoidance rather than explicit cost reduction. Productivity gains are often reinvested into further technology modernisation, data infrastructure, cybersecurity and compliance, while improvements in fraud detection and risk analytics primarily enhance earnings resilience rather than driving immediate margin expansion.
Management commentaries across Asian banks consistently highlight operational improvements and strategic importance, but limited short-term impact on reported cost ratios.

title_content.content: 5. Medium-term: AI is the largest remaining cost lever

paragraph_content.content: Looking ahead, we believe AI nonetheless represents the most meaningful remaining cost lever for Asian banks over the medium term. Banking operations typically account for 60–70% of the overall cost base, making end-to-end operational AI a potentially powerful driver of efficiency once scaled.

As banks move beyond the initial high-capex phase of building data and AI infrastructure, digital labour can scale at very low marginal cost, allowing revenues to grow without a commensurate increase in headcount or physical infrastructure. Early examples demonstrate the scale of potential operational displacement once AI adoption reaches maturity.

Overall, AI is shifting from a narrative enhancer to a delivery obligation for Asian banks. While near-term financial benefits appear limited, we believe the medium-term opportunity to reshape cost structures is substantial. Execution, rather than intent or messaging, will ultimately determine which banks emerge as the beneficiaries of the next phase of efficiency improvement.

title_content.content: Asian banks are facing structural headwinds on revenue

paragraph_content.content: In our Q-Series published last year (Silver wave: How an ageing population is reshaping Asian finance), we discussed how Asia is undergoing a demographic transformation, with the population anticipated to peak in the next 15 years and by 2050, the population aged 65+ is expected to double. We believe these changes will lead to a rising dependency ratio and have a substantial effect on Asian economies and banking systems.

title_content.content: Net interest income is on a structural downtrend from an ageing demographic

paragraph_content.content: Our analysis identified three significant megatrends stemming from an ageing population. The first is a reduction in consumer savings, followed by a shift in asset allocation from deposits to investments, and lastly, a deceleration in the growth of consumer loans. We believe these megatrends will have a direct effect on Asian banks' profitability and their strategies.

Firstly, as both deposits and lending activities decelerate, with lending experiencing a more pronounced slowdown, net interest margins (NIM) of these banks are expected to enter a long-term decline, weighing on net interest income (NII).

title_content.content: What led to the lower opex/assets ratio over the past 20y?

paragraph_content.content: Operating expenses are usually broken down into 2 broad categories for banks – 1) staff costs (e.g. salaries, bonuses, employee benefits) and 2) other operating expenses (e.g. administrative expenses, branch and office rent, IT expenses, marketing costs).

Our analysis of the Asian banks suggests staff costs account for slightly less than 50% of total opex (49% of total opex in 2025), though the contribution to total opex could range between 30-65% among markets which we discuss in greater detail in a later section.

title_content.content: Are there significant differences on the cost-to-income ratio?

paragraph_content.content: On a cost-to-income (CIR) basis, we find little differences between DM and EM banks, both of which were around the 45-50% range in 2025.

However, EM banks managed to lower their CIR over the past 20y, while CIR increased for the DM banks. On an Asian banks level, CIR was around 46% in 2025, declining 1ppt over the past 20y, driven by a 7ppt decline for the EM banks offsetting a 5ppt increase for the DM banks.

This is interesting, as the common perception has been that EM banks should operate with higher CIR, given their need for extensive branch networks to reach underserved segments, as well as generally lower operating efficiencies due to more limited technological investment. However, our findings challenge this view, with EM banks demonstrating CIRs broadly comparable to those in developed markets.
What explains this apparent divergence from conventional thinking?

title_content.content: Why are China, Vietnam, and Hong Kong (domestic) banks able to run at sub-40% cost-income ratio?

paragraph_content.content: We have been asked by several investors in the past why China, Vietnam, and Hong Kong (domestic) banks are able to run at sub-40% cost-income ratio (CIR) when their EM and DM counterparts are running at 44%/49% respectively.

China banks: Chinese banks reported around 38% CIR in 2025. Average CIR from 2014-24 was around 35%. Higher CIR in 2025 was driven by faster growth in costs relative to revenue growth. Nevertheless, CIR was still comparatively lower compared to the EM banks average (38% in China vs 44% in EM). Looking at costs from an ROA perspective, China banks also performed better (ie. lower ratios) on both staff costs/assets and other opex/assets. This could likely be due to China banks' relatively stronger tech and digital capabilities, driving better operating efficiencies and lower costs (measured on both CIR and ROA basis).

Vietnam banks: Vietnamese banks recorded around 30% CIR in 2025, steadily declined from mid-40% in 2015. We believe this is a reflection of stronger revenue growth (high credit growth and fee growth, offsetting NIM pressure) relative to costs growth. Not only are Vietnamese banks performing better on CIR (compared to EM), they also outperformed (ie. lower ratios) on both staff costs/assets and other opex/assets, albeit less so than Chinese banks. Total opex/assets ratios were 1.3% in Vietnam, compared to 0.7% in China and 1.8% for EM banks. This suggests the Vietnam banks' relatively lower CIR of 30% was attributed more to stronger revenues (compared to EM), but likely relatively less due to tech and digital capabilities as with the Chinese banks.

Hong Kong banks: The key driver of the lower CIR is attributed to BOCHK, which reported a 24% CIR 2025. The other HK (domestic) bank, BEA, reported a CIR of 47% in 2025 which is close to the DM average. BOCHK has also impressively achieved positive JAWS with over the past few years with CIR averaging 29% over 2014-24. We attribute the strong operating efficiency to the bank's scale in Hong Kong (16-17% market share), and costs optimisation efforts by centralizing back-office operations in lower-cost regional hubs such as Nanning and deploying AI and robotic process automation to maximise back-office efficiency.
Diving deeper into the opex breakdown, DM banks' staff costs/revenue ratio was roughly 24% on average in 2025, while this was slightly lower for EM banks at around 19%.

This is an interesting observation as the general view has been that DM banks should have lower staff costs/revenue ratio as they have invested more in technology which should yield better operating efficiencies and lower staff count (through increased automation and lesser need for branches). However, this finding appears to be at odds with the common perception whereby DM banks are actually running at higher staff costs/revenue ratio than the EM banks.
Cost-to-income ratios for the both DM and EM banks have declined over the past 20y, and ranged around 45-46% in 2025

We think this could be due to a few possible reasons: 1) higher wages in DM markets relative to EM markets which offsets the lower staff count in general, 2) costs savings on lower administrative staff count is replaced by higher number of tech employees which generally earn higher wages, and 3) technological investments takes time to yield significant costs savings given the legacy banking systems which have to be replaced.

title_content.content: Banking consolidation has helped in lowering cost pressures

paragraph_content.content: With increasing revenue pressures facing the banking sector, and the need for continued and higher costs investments (higher tech and regulatory costs), we have seen banking consolidation in several markets over the past 20y.
China has the largest number of licensed banking institutions among the Asian banking markets with close to 4,300 banks as of 2024 (-6% since 2018).

Indonesia has the second highest number of banks with close to 1,500 banks as of 2024, despite the total count down around 25% over the past 20y. We also note how the total bank count in the Philippines has halved over the past 25y to slightly more than 450 banks in 2025.

Other markets with a high number of banking institutions are India (208 scheduled banks), Hong Kong (149 banks), Singapore (133 banks), and Japan (107 banks). Note: Definition of banking institutions may vary across markets – definitions can be found in the grey text box below.

Nevertheless, the key insight in this section is that in most markets the number of licensed banking institutions was generally stable to declining over the past 5 years. Markets that saw a relatively larger decline in banks were the Philippines (-13% since 2020), China, Hong Kong, Australia, and Thailand (all -7% over the past 5y).

title_content.content: Branch rationalisation initiatives are also underway

paragraph_content.content: Based on data from the World Bank (latest data as of 2023), most markets in Asia have seen a decline in branch penetration (measured by the number of branches per 100k adults) from 2018-23, apart from India (+1%) and Japan (flat), which likely contributed to savings on total opex. Markets that saw the largest decline in branch penetration from 2018-23 were Australia (-39%), Indonesia (-27%), Thailand (-26%), and Singapore (-25%).

On an absolute basis, branch penetration was the highest in Japan (34 branches per 100k adults) in 2023, followed closely by Hong Kong (18 branches) and Australia (17 branches). On the other end, Vietnam has the lowest branch penetration (3 branches per 100k adults), followed by Singapore (6 branches), and Thailand (8 branches).

title_content.content: Even as total employee headcount has generally risen...

paragraph_content.content: While the total number of branches in most Asian markets have declined over the past 5y, the total number of bank employees have increased for most markets.

This could have been driven by a shift in employee mix from customer-facing branch tellers in the past to increasingly more back-end tech support staff over the years. Furthermore, the increase in overall headcount could have been driven by the need for more technological investments and thus higher tech headcount among banks over the past few years, given increasing competition from fintechs and increasing demand from end consumers for better digital offerings.

paragraph_content.content: This relationship appears to be more driven by changes in staff cost structure (Figure 39). Technology investments reduce reliance on higher-cost front-end roles by automating customer-facing and manual processes, even as overall headcount continues to grow (see the section above). The resulting shift toward more back-end and operational roles, which are typically lower-cost, helps contain personnel expenses and contributes to lower overall cost intensity.

This relationship is more pronounced in emerging markets such as Vietnam and the Philippines. This is intuitive, as these markets generally started with lower operating efficiency, leaving greater scope to capture meaningful cost savings through higher technology investments.

We believe that continued technology investment should further enhance operating efficiency, particularly across emerging markets, over the medium term. To date, most tech spending has been directed toward digitalising legacy systems, enhancing digital capabilities (e.g. retail and consumer banking interfaces), and strengthening cybersecurity. Looking ahead, we see artificial intelligence as the next potential driver of operating efficiency gains.

Over time, we believe AI is likely to emerge as a key differentiator among banks: those that invest early and meaningfully in AI, and, importantly, foster an organisational culture that supports experimentation and rapid implementation, are likely to be best positioned to translate technological capability into sustainable efficiency gains and competitive advantage. title_content.content: Will AI drive better costs efficiencies for the Asian banks?

paragraph_content.content: Having discussed the key cost drivers – and the extent to which they have only partially offset structural revenue pressures for Asian banks – the question then becomes whether AI can emerge as the next structural driver of operating efficiency.

AI is increasingly viewed as a strategic necessity, with banks that fail to evolve toward AI-native operating models at risk of falling behind on both cost efficiency and competitive capability. Against this backdrop, adoption is accelerating across the region, with many Asian banks moving beyond pilot programmes toward scaled, enterprise-wide deployment of GenAI and agentic AI across core operations.

These efforts are primarily focused on three broad areas so far: 1) enhancing customer experience through personalization; 2) driving productivity gains in internal workflows like software engineering and document processing; and 3) fortifying defensive moats through real-time fraud detection and risk analytics. However, the financial impact of these use cases is uneven across categories.

title_content.content: From a P&L perspective, the financial impact of these initiatives is asymmetric across these three areas:

paragraph_content.content: Investments in customer personalization are best viewed as defensive rather than revenue accretive, as such capabilities have increasingly become table stakes across the industry. While improved engagement and cross-sell are often cited benefits, the more tangible outcome is the prevention of customer attrition and share loss, in our view. As personalization becomes ubiquitous, its absence is more likely to result in revenue leakage than its presence driving incremental topline growth.

Productivity-oriented use cases, particularly in software development, operations, and document processing, offer clearer scope for cost efficiencies in the medium term, although quantification remains challenging at this stage. We believe gains are likely to accrue gradually through headcount cost avoidance, faster turnaround times, and reduced error rates rather than explicit cost out. As such, near-term margin uplift may be limited, with benefits manifesting more as a structural hedge against operating cost inflation over the medium term.

Lastly, AI investments in fraud detection and risk analytics have a more direct bearing on earnings stability rather than earnings expansion. While improved data ingestion and real-time analytics could modestly enhance credit underwriting outcomes, we believe the primary benefit lies in mitigating downside risks – lower fraud losses, earlier identification of asset quality deterioration, and reduced tail-risk events. In this sense, these capabilities help contain potential future costs that could otherwise materialise in the absence of such investments, supporting more resilient returns through the cycle.
As such, we believe the benefits of AI adoption are currently more operational than financial, with limited translation into reported cost ratios.

title_content.content: Banks are spending more on AI than they are saving, at present

paragraph_content.content: Despite these early operational breakthroughs – and we would expect meaningful costs savings in the medium term given that operations can represent ~60-70% of a bank's costs base (based on the McKinsey report here) – there is currently a noticeable financialization gap where AI has not yet translated into material costs improvements in many instances. This is evident in banks commentaries (particularly HSBC) summarised in the tables below.

The key reason behind this is that while localized efficiency gains are significant – such as reducing lending decision times or automating customer messaging – these are not yet headcount-cut stories in most cases (see our discussion on headcount in the section above). They are primarily capacity-release stories (same headcount, higher throughput)

Furthermore, the resulting cost savings today are likely being largely reinvested in additional capital expenditure required for larger data infrastructure, technological upgrades, cybersecurity, and compliance.

Consequently, many banks report that production use cases have not yet delivered significant financial impacts, as they prioritize reinvesting these gains into further technological modernization to remain competitive against peers and digital-native disruptors.

title_content.content: Medium term: From implementation to costs savings

paragraph_content.content: Looking ahead, we think the potential for AI to drive material cost savings for banks in the medium term remains strong given the large amount of data and human capital. Furthermore, based on the findings from McKinsey (report here), operations can represent ~60–70% of a bank's cost base, making operational AI the biggest cost lever for banks if scaled end-to-end.

For example, ICBC in China has said that it has reached a milestone where the workload handled by AI is equivalent to more than 40,000 full-time employees, illustrating the substantial scale of operational displacement possible.

Furthermore, as banks move past the initial high capex phase of building data infrastructure, these "digital workers" can scale with very low marginal cost, eventually allowing banks to scale their revenues without a linear increase in headcount or physical infrastructure.

title_content.content: From qualitative statements to hard numbers

paragraph_content.content: As investor expectations mature, banks will need to adapt by doing more than talking about AI. The bar is rising from signalling intent to proving impact, with greater emphasis on measurable P&L outcomes and strong governance. Institutions that fail to translate investment into demonstrable financial or risk-mitigating benefits risk losing credibility, as AI narratives without execution risk being increasingly discounted by the market.

Put differently, AI is transitioning from a narrative enhancer to a delivery obligation, with execution risk becoming as relevant as technological capability. Over time, differences in AI readiness and execution could become a key driver of cost and valuation divergence across Asian banks (please refer to our companion APAC Focus note here).

title_content.content: Valuation Method and Risk Statement

paragraph_content.content: The main risk for Asian banks is inflation in countries with current account deficits and low FX reserves as higher interest rates would hurt margins for banks with high LDRs and hurt credit quality. Also, asymmetric increases in deposit rates and fewer rises in lending rates could hurt current high loan margins. Banks with equity/asset ratios below 5% and ROAs below 1% are vulnerable to economic and regulatory risk, especially if still growing loans by more than 15% per annum, as they will encounter capital shortages.
